chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 221 to 240: short akam poems of waiting and lost beauty, in which the mullai season arrives without the man (221, 234, 240), the friend demands back the beauty the man has consumed (236, 238), the woman's wasted body leaves no shame to keep (239), and onlookers credit fate with marrying childhood rivals (229).

221.reading: The woman says he has not come though the mullai has bloomed: the goatherd who leaves his lambs, comes into the village with milk and goes back with gruel, wears nothing on his head but small green mullai buds.
221.nuance: The season's proof is put on the humblest head: even the goatherd is crowned with the buds the man was to come back by. The goatherd also comes and goes back every day; a reader may hear a reproach in that, but nothing in the poem draws it, so the herdsman stays scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits through the season he promised to return in

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

222.reading: The man says that in the water-play she takes the head of the raft when he does and the tail when he does, and if he lets the raft go and drifts with the stream she will seemingly come there too, she whose rain-cool eyes have corners red as the streaks of a wet jasmine bud and who is like a tender shoot drops have fallen on.
222.nuance: The doubled lines (தலைப்புணை ... கடைப்புணை) move the way she moves, copying his every hold; the third conditional pushes the play to the point of risk, letting go into the current, and still she follows. The bud of the rainy-season jasmine is a mullai thing in a kurinji poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the union of lovers who cannot be parted

comparisons.tenor: the red-streaked corners of her eyes
the girl, fresh and tender

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

223.reading: The woman reminds her friend that the friend kept saying 'let us go' to the festival that filled the big town, and that on that day, here, he gave her the bird-scaring rattles and tender leaves, said falsely that they suited her, and took the fine beauty her mother had guarded, so that she is now as she is.
223.nuance: She turns the blame on the friend: while the friend wanted the town festival, the union happened 'here', in the field, through small gifts of the millet-guard's own tools. Line 3 (நல்லோர் நல்ல பலவாற் றில்ல) is hard to construe, so who 'the good ones' are is not fixed.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet-guarding rattles of the hill field

224.reading: The woman tells her friend that brooding on the cruelty of the man who went down the long road of forking paths makes her sleepless sickness worse than sickness, and that like a mute man who saw at night a cow suffering in a well she cannot bear the pain and cannot speak it.
224.nuance: The simile has two sufferers: the cow in the well and the mute who sees it and can neither help nor call for help; she is the second, so the pain is doubled by being unspeakable. உயர்திணை, 'of the higher class', marks him as human, set against the animal he watches.

thinai_evidence.note: she suffers the absence of the man who went on the hard road

comparisons.vehicle: கூவற் குராலான் படுதுயர் இராவிற் கண்ட உயர்திணை ஊமன்
comparisons.tenor: the woman who sees her own pain and cannot speak it

225.reading: The friend tells the man of the great-rock country, where a she-elephant eats the millet in the yard while her calf drinks at her rich udder, that if he does not forget kindness, as a king forgets the help he received in ruin once he has gained the glory of the throne, then the girl's thick soft hair, like the spread tail of a proud peacock, is his.
225.nuance: The gift of her hair is conditional: it is his only if he is not the ungrateful king, so the friend presses for marriage by naming the vice in advance. The she-elephant eating the household's millet while she suckles has been read as the lover taking freely what is not yet his, but the scene gives only one pair, so it stays scene (a near miss on ullurai condition 3).

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant in the millet yard of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the lover who might forget the help of the girl's love once he has what he wants
the girl's thick soft hair

226.reading: The woman tells her friend that her flower-like eyes, her shoulders lovely as bamboo and her forehead that could be mistaken for the crescent were truly fine before she laughed with the lord of the wide-water shore, where every night white screwpine buds struck by the waves open like herons.
226.nuance: The praise of her beauty is all in the past tense (நல்லமன், 'were good indeed'): the catalogue of eyes, shoulders and brow is an inventory of what she has lost. The screwpine bud that looks like a heron is a thing that seems what it is not; some read the hero's look of constancy in it, but the poem gives no second pair, so it stays a simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine and waves of the shore

comparisons.tenor: her eyes
her shoulders
her forehead
the white screwpine bud as it opens

227.reading: The friend says that here in the seaside grove the chariot-man drove away from, there are even stubby neythal flowers with their broad petals cut off, sliced by the bright face of the golden-rimmed wheel that looks like a wrought jewel.
227.nuance: The poem says only that there is evidence: the lilies cut by a chariot wheel prove the man came to the grove. To whom the friend shows this sign, and why (to tell the heroine he came, or to let the household learn of the affair), the poem does not say, so the situation is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flowers of the seaside grove

comparisons.tenor: the golden rim of the chariot wheel

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

228.reading: The woman says that though the man of the cool sea left us and belongs to a far country, he is near to her heart, in the land where, they say, the waves come up to the yard of the little hamlet by the seaside grove and go back, and the ripe screwpine bud opens its petals like a heron preening its feathers.
228.nuance: She knows his land only by report (என்ப, 'they say'), and what she chooses to repeat is the coming and going of the waves. The far country and the near heart are set side by side (நெடுஞ்சேண் ... நெஞ்சிற்கு அணியர) with no complaint.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine, the grove and the waves of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the screwpine bud opening its sheaths

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

iraicchi.act: the waves come up to the doorstep of his hamlet and go back again
iraicchi.sense: even the sea of his own country comes and returns, so his going is not the end of his coming

229.reading: Onlookers say that the two who once fought small senseless fights, he pulling her plaited hair and she pulling his thin tuft while their loving nurses tried and failed to stop them, have been shown the joy of marriage by fate, which has done well to join them like a garland of paired flowers.
229.nuance: The childhood fights are the evidence of the match: those who could not be kept apart even to fight are now joined by பால், the portion fate deals. The poem has nothing of the paalai land; its paalai filing presumably follows the onlookers' frame of the couple seen on the road.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem gives no land or season; paalai is the colophon's

comparisons.tenor: the couple joined in marriage

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the onlookers address fate (பால்), which the last line calls காட்டியோயே

230.reading: The friend asks the woman whether she herself, in her simplicity, did something to hurt that noble man when they met, for the lord of the shore is not one to resolve on such a thing, yet he no longer knows the way of coming, as he did in those few days, over the water path where fierce sharks move.
230.nuance: The friend blames herself (யான் என் பேதைமையால்) rather than the man, a polite way of saying he has stopped coming without accusing him; the shark-haunted water reminds that his earlier visits braved danger, so their stopping cannot be fear.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the shark-haunted waters

231.reading: The woman says that though they live in one town he does not come to her street, and if he comes he does not embrace her fully, but passes by without looking, as one passes a stranger's burning-ground; and her desire, having killed shame and lost good sense, has gone far like an arrow loosed from the bow.
231.nuance: The stranger's burning-ground is a place one passes with averted eyes, so the simile says he treats her as an unlucky sight. The closing turns from him to herself: her own desire has already gone, past shame and sense, and cannot be called back. Line 6 reads கணியிற், where the sense wants கணையின், 'arrow'.

thinai_evidence.note: the neglect of a man who lives in the same town

comparisons.tenor: the man passing her by without a look
her desire, gone beyond recall

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

232.reading: The friend asks whether they have not thought of us, or whether, thinking, they do not come for lack of a fitting chance, those who crossed the hill of dark groves where a dark-necked stag, weary for want of the marul to graze, sleeps in the striped shade of a yaa tree left after a mortar-legged elephant broke and ate it.
232.nuance: The two questions give the absent man two excuses, forgetting or lack of chance, and the friend leaves both open. The stag that sleeps in the thin, striped shade left over by an elephant shows a land where even rest is a remnant; it carries a mood and does nothing a lover does, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the absence of those who crossed the hills

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's legs, thick as a mortar

233.reading: The man says that the town of the father of the girl with rows of small bangles is in the forest that has met the rains, where bright konrai flowers spread in small wide pits dug up by digging, like opened gold-filled caskets of the rich, and where the rice left after water-poured offerings to the great knows no limit to anyone.
233.nuance: He praises her by her father's house: its leftovers are shared with everyone without limit, which makes her family the generous household the ethical books describe. The konrai fallen into pits like gold in caskets makes the rainy forest itself look rich. Whether he speaks returning or on the way to ask for her, the poem does not say.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest that has met the rains

comparisons.tenor: the golden konrai flowers lying in the pits

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

234.reading: The woman says that those who call evening the hour when the sky reddens as the sun goes and the mullai blooms as the light fails are confused: for those without a partner, the great breaking dawn when the crested cock calls through the tall house is evening too, and so is the day.
234.nuance: She uses the definition of evening (மாலை என்மனார், 'so they say') as a learned premise and refutes it from experience: the hour is not fixed by the sky but by the absence of a companion. It is a poem about the mutal itself, the time proper to mullai, overturned.

thinai_evidence.note: evening, the mullai hour, made the frame of her waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

235.reading: The man asks the north wind to guard it: near the high rock with its pure white waterfall hanging like a snake's cast skin, the town of his good woman is a grass-thatched hut in whose yard herds of marai deer feed on nelli.
235.nuance: Her town is only a grass hut, but he names it as the one place he wants protected. The north wind, which brings the cold season, is asked to be gentle where she is: the season that makes her suffer is the one he appeals to. Everything he sees in her place is kurinji; the paalai is only in his being away.

thinai_evidence.note: the man far from her asks the wind to keep her place

comparisons.tenor: the white waterfall

236.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool sea, where a stray stork roosts on the low branch of a punnai standing on the shore of sand heaped like hills, to let the day of his leaving come if he has agreed to it, but first to give back the beauty he has consumed and then go.
236.nuance: The demand is impossible on purpose: beauty that has been 'eaten' cannot be handed back, so the only way to settle the debt is not to leave. The friend speaks in the girl's person (என் நலன்).

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, the stork and the cool sea

comparisons.tenor: the heaped sand of the shore

ullurai.tenor: the man who lodged for a while with the girl and may leave her

pairs.situation: the man is a passing stranger, not one who stays
he has rested on her and enjoyed her beauty
the girl who bent to him and has nothing to hold him by

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a neythal stork and punnai of the poem's own shore (porul 7.27)

237.reading: The man says that though his heart, which knows no fear and has embraced its beloved, has left him for her, it matters little if the bond of his hands, all that is left, should loosen; for the space between the two of them is very great, and he cannot count what now stands in the way of their embrace: groves where the killing tiger roams to the right, roaring like the waves of the great sea.
237.nuance: The heart has already crossed to her; only the body, held back by its grip, is here, and the obstacle between them is reckoned in forests and tigers. Lines 1 to 3 are compressed and line 2 is a repaired reading, so the exact turn of the argument (whose hands, what bond) is uncertain; மலைவு in line 7 may mean the hills between them or the obstruction itself.

thinai_evidence.note: the distance of a man gone from her

comparisons.tenor: the tiger's roar

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

238.reading: The friend tells the lord of the fields to give back her beauty, which was like Tondi, where girls with bright bangles play at sand-houses after laying to sleep on the ridge of the ripe paddy the black-cored pestle that pounded green flattened rice, and then go, keeping his oath.
238.nuance: The pestle 'put to sleep' on the field ridge and the girls at play describe a town so secure its work stops for games; that ease is what her beauty was. 'Go, keeping your oath' is bitter: the oath he swore is what he is breaking by going.

thinai_evidence.note: the paddy ridges and the lord of the fields

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, rich and at ease like the port town

239.reading: The woman tells her friend that her bangles have slipped and her shoulders wasted, so is there any shame left to give up for the lord of the hill hedged with bamboo, where the short-winged bee sucking the fragrant pollen of the swaying kanthal that scents the hill at the cleft looks like a gem spat out by a snake?
239.nuance: Her body has already published what modesty would hide, so there is no shame left to lose by speaking; the line prepares the move from secrecy to disclosure. The bee at the kanthal, a creature on a bloom shaped like a snake's hood, is a dangerous-seeming beauty; some read the lover in it, but no second pair is given, so it stays a simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the kanthal and bamboo of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the dark bee in the red kanthal bloom

240.reading: The woman tells her friend to see how, on top of the north wind's coming, when the many bright avarai flowers like parrots' beaks crowd on the bush with mullai buds like a wild cat's teeth, at evening his tall blue hill shows like a ship sinking into the sea and then vanishes, so that her sickness strikes.
240.nuance: The one thing of his she can see is his hill, and evening takes even that: it does not vanish at once but sinks like a ship, a slow loss watched to the end. The sinking ship is a neythal thing in a mullai poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the north wind and evening of the waiting season

comparisons.tenor: the avarai flowers
the mullai buds
his hill fading from sight at evening

links.note: In Akananuru 274 the returning man says her town lies in the rainy scrub where a lone herdsman stands in the drizzle with his lambs; in Kuruntokai 221 the waiting woman sees the goatherd with his lambs crowned with mullai buds and says the man has not come.
links.teaches: The herdsman of the mullai scrub is the season's witness from both sides: on the man's road he marks the way home, at the woman's door he wears the proof that the promised season has come without the man, so one figure serves as sign of return or of broken promise.

links.note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life; in Kuruntokai 222 the man says she takes the head of the raft when he does, the tail when he does, and would follow him into the current.
links.teaches: The couplet names the inseparability as a metaphor, and the poem shows how a lover knows it: she mirrors his every movement in play and would follow him into danger, so the body-and-life bond is proved by action before it is stated.

links.note: Purananuru 34 states that there is no expiation for killing a benefit and binds the poet to praise the king who fed the bards; Kuruntokai 225 makes a king who forgets, once enthroned, the help he had in ruin the type of ingratitude the lover must not imitate.
links.teaches: The puram poem casts the king as the benefactor to whom gratitude is owed, while the akam friend can cite the king who forgets his helpers as a familiar figure, so the same norm of gratitude was also turned against kings, and borrowed to bind a lover to marriage.

links.note: Kural 110: there is escape for every other killing of good, none for one who kills a benefit; in Kuruntokai 225 the friend promises the girl's hair to the man only if he does not forget kindness as an enthroned king does.
links.teaches: The Kural's absolute rule becomes a condition of marriage in the poem: the friend uses ingratitude, the one unpardonable fault, to define in advance what deserting the girl would be.

links.note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes to seek when the lover is inside it; Kuruntokai 228: though he left for a far country, he is near to her heart.
links.teaches: The same indwelling is used two ways: the couplet makes it a reason to scold the restless heart, while the poem makes it a consolation that cancels the distance, so the lover in the heart can either rebuke longing or quiet it.

links.note: Kuruntokai 40 marvels that two whose mothers, fathers and selves were strangers have hearts mixed like rain in red earth; Kuruntokai 229 marvels that two who fought as children under their nurses' eyes have been joined in marriage, and credits fate (பால்).
links.teaches: The anthology explains a match both between strangers and between childhood neighbours, and in each case puts the cause outside the families: loving hearts mixing on their own in 40, fate's apportioning in 229, so union by kin arrangement is the case neither poem celebrates.

links.note: Kural 1247: the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; Kuruntokai 231: neglected by the man in her own town, she says her desire, having killed shame and lost good sense, has gone far like a loosed arrow.
links.teaches: The couplet presents a choice still open between desire and shame, while the poem shows it already made and past recall, desire having killed shame on its own, so the Kural's dilemma is the moment before the poem's confession.

links.note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftover (மிச்சில்) needs sowing at all; Kuruntokai 233 praises her father's town where the leftover (மிச்சில்) of rice poured out for the great is shared with all without limit.
links.teaches: The love poet measures a bride's family by the very household ethic the Kural states, even with its word for the leftover, so the hospitality rule was already a mark of a good marriage before it was a maxim about prosperity.

links.note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 234: for those without a partner the dawn and the day are evening too.
links.teaches: The couplet keeps evening as the climax of a daily growth, while the poem refuses any such gradation and makes every hour evening, so on one reading the parted woman has no easier morning at all, which the Kural's flower image allows.

links.note: Kural 1183: the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange; Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the man that if he means to leave he must first give back the beauty he has consumed.
links.teaches: The couplet records the exchange as done, and the poem turns the same commercial idea into a demand for repayment that cannot be met, which makes it an argument that he must stay.

links.note: Kural 1108: an embrace so close not even the wind can part it is sweet to two who desire each other; Kuruntokai 237: the man far away says he cannot count what now stands between their embrace, groves where tigers roar.
links.teaches: Read together, the measure of separation is the same embrace the couplet praises: where once not even a breeze passed between them, now forests and tigers do, so the poem's distance is felt as a gap inside the embrace.

links.note: In Akananuru 60 the friend warns the hero not to crush the bangle of a girl fine as Porayan's Tondi; in Kuruntokai 238 the friend tells the lord of the fields to give back a beauty that was like Tondi and go.
links.teaches: Both friends price the girl's beauty by the Chera port of Tondi, one before harm, as a warning, and one after, as a demand for restitution, so the town's fame served as the standard of a beauty that can be damaged and must be repaid.

links.note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders lose their old beauty and her bangles slip; Kuruntokai 239: her bangles have slipped and her shoulders wasted, so is there shame left to give up?
links.teaches: The couplet lists the slipping bangles as a sign of grief, while the poem draws from the same sign a conclusion: since the body has already told, modesty has nothing left to hide, so the wasting licenses the woman to speak out.

links.note: Kuruntokai 234 says that for those without a partner every hour is evening; Kuruntokai 240 shows one evening's work, as the north wind blows and his hill sinks from view like a ship.
links.teaches: Together they show why evening is the worst hour: in 234 it is a state that swallows all hours, in 240 it is the moment the last visible trace of him, his hill, is taken away, so the evening's pain is the loss of sight of him.

kuruntokai:223 line 3 (நல்லோர் நல்ல பலவாற் றில்ல) is hard to construe; the reading is uncertain.

kuruntokai:221-240: the colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so thurai_akam addressees are taken from vocatives in the poems where present and given as pira otherwise, and occasion.words is null.
